newsitem.title: UK: SAfrica, Namibia uranium mines mulling more output.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica, Namibia uranium mines mulling more output.

text.p: Rising uranium prices may soon tempt the mines in southern Africa to raise output and rival the biggest producers, say analysts and industry officials.

South Africa has abundant reserves but limited production capacity and neighbour Namibia, although a substantial source, is not yet in the same league as Canada and Uzbekistan. It would only raise production if assured of long-term contracts based on prices continuing to extend a recent rally.

Stockpiles at most Western nuclear utilities have now run down to equal only about a year's demand. Analysts expect new production to pick up to fill more than the present 55 percent of the global requirement of around 64,000 tonnes.
Martin Taylor, an analyst at the London-based Uranium Institute, said combined volume from South Africa and Namibia already put southern Africa as a whole among top producers.
"Our expectations is that production in these two countries will gradually increase. It is unlikely to be a dramatic increase," Taylor said.
Namibia produced 2,366 tonnes in 1995, up from the 2,252 the previous year. South Africa produced 1,906 tonnes in 1994 which is the last year for which firm figures are available.
The Uranium Institute has calculated that there are only about 80,000 tonnes of uranium stocks left worldwide in Western nuclear utilities, as the market recovers from a slump in demand.

The slump followed the end of the Cold War and the subsequent fall in demand for weapons-grade uranium for use in nuclear weapons. In addition, less nuclear plants were built after accidents at Three Mile Island and Chernobyl. But in the past two years, world uranium prices have almost doubled to around $16 a pound.
Any increased demand for new output promises succour to a South African industry particularly hard hit by the slump in the world market.
South African mining giant, Anglo American Corp which produces around 60 percent of the country's uranium as a by-product of gold mining said it did not foresee any imminent increase in output.

"There are very large uranium reserves but these are very low-grade ore and would require very much higher prices to turn to general account," Anglo's Gold and Uranium Division marketing director Kelvin Williams said.
"While some upgrading of output from existing plants is possible, the plants that remain are otherwise at pretty well full capacity.
"So to increase uranium production substantially in simple terms, you would need to built at least one new plant," Williams said.
A new plant similiar to the one currently in operation at Anglo's Vaal Reefs Exploration and Mining Co Ltd would cost in the region of 750 million rand.
In the decade since 1984, South African uranium production declined sharply which led to the closure of 13 plants.
The South African Minerals Bureau said only four producers were extracting uranium from five plants at present.
Namibia's major producer of primary uranium, Rossing Uranium, was currently operating almost 50 percent below its production capacity, Rossing managing director Andrew Hope said.
He said Rossing, of which 60 percent is owned by Anglo-Australian mining group RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd, would consider lifting production if it secured more long-term contracts.
The Rossing operation was designed to produce around 4,500 tonnes of uranium but 1995 production only stood at 2,336 tonnes, Hope said.
"We certainly see the market improving but it remains in the early days".
